summary:
Goa is a state of India and stands under the national framework on transgender recognition, identity documents and criminal law. No Goan statute diverging from that national position is on file.

Marriage and partnership recognition in Goa is set by the Goa Civil Code, a state-level instrument that defines marriage as between a man and a woman and gives no legal recognition to same-sex marriage or civil union. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status cannot have that relationship recognised in Goa, and the code applies in this state rather than the personal-law system used elsewhere in India.

Goa has no state-level anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation. Protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity in Goa rests on the national Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which applies in the state.

On 7 May 2025 the state government constituted a 14-member Model Transgender Welfare Board, chaired by the Chief Secretary, under the 2019 Act and the 2020 Rules, with a mandate covering implementation of welfare schemes and safeguarding transgender persons' rights in healthcare, education, employment and housing.

Administrative recognition in Goa lags the resident population. The 2011 census recorded 398 transgender people in Goa; by 2024 only 12 transgender people were registered on the state's electoral rolls, the first registrations having taken place in 2022. A trans visitor dealing with state offices should expect registration and documentation processes that have only recently begun to include transgender residents.

Harassment of transgender people in Goan institutions is documented. A 2018 study by the Goa Livelihoods Forum found that 87 per cent of transgender respondents had dropped out of school because of harassment. The figure describes the state's social climate for transgender residents rather than a specific risk to short-stay visitors, but it records a local pattern of harassment in schools and comparable settings.

No bill on relationship recognition has been introduced in the Goa legislature.
tangentialFactors:
Marriage recognition in Goa is governed by a state-level code rather than by national statute, so the position on partnership recognition for a trans visitor is set by Goan law and is not altered by national litigation on marriage equality.

The 2011 census count of 398 transgender people in Goa sits within a national count of 487,803. Raw counts track population size, and Goa's small total reflects the size of the state rather than a lower or higher level of risk.

The distance between the 398 people recorded in the 2011 census and the 12 registered on the electoral rolls by 2024 is an indicator of administrative recognition and registration practice in Goa. It is not a count of the state's transgender population.

No reports of police conduct toward transgender people specific to Goa were located, and no assessment of how Goan authorities enforce the non-discrimination provisions of the 2019 Act is sourced. The national record on police conduct and court-issued protections is carried by the national assessment.

The operational record of the Model Transgender Welfare Board since its constitution on 7 May 2025 is not sourced: no information was located on meetings held, schemes delivered or budget allocated.

Whether Goa operates transgender-specific shelter, healthcare or custodial provision beyond the board's stated mandate is not sourced.

The 2011 census is the most recent population count for transgender people in Goa available in the sources reviewed; no later count is sourced.
